title: White-tailed deer
def: The white-tailed deer is the common deer of the East, brown with a white belly and a tail it raises like a white flag when alarmed.
look: brown coat, white underside, tail raised like a white flag
bucks carry antlers from late summer to winter
use: Deer are the main big-game animal in New England; check your state's season and tag rules before hunting.
not: Do not approach a fawn lying alone; the doe is usually nearby. Watch for deer on roads at dawn and dusk.

title: Moose
def: The moose is the largest deer, with a long face, a hanging dewlap, and broad flat antlers on bulls.
look: huge with a long face, dewlap, and broad flat antlers on bulls
dark body on long pale legs
use: Watch from at least 50 yards (about 45 m). If one lays its ears back or raises its hackles, back away and put a tree between you.
not: Do not approach a cow with a calf or a bull in fall rut. Moose cause serious crashes at night on Maine roads.

title: Elk
def: The elk is a large deer with a pale rump, a dark neck, and branching antlers on bulls.
look: large with a pale rump and branching antlers
bugling calls in fall
use: Elk are rare in New England; a big brown deer there is more likely a moose or white-tailed deer.
not: Do not approach; bulls in rut and cows with calves charge.

title: Black bear
def: The black bear is the only bear in the East, black or brown, with a straight face profile and no shoulder hump.
look: black or brown with a straight muzzle and no shoulder hump
tall pointed ears
short curved claws
use: Make noise on the trail, store food and trash away from camp, and if you meet one, stand tall, talk firmly, and back away slowly.
not: Never run or climb a tree to escape. If a black bear attacks, fight back. Keep distance, never run, store food away from camp.

title: Coyote
def: The eastern coyote is a slim, dog-like wild canine with a bushy tail carried low and pointed ears.
look: slim dog-like with a bushy low tail and pointed ears
yips and howls at night
use: If one comes close, make yourself big, shout, and throw something toward it.
not: Do not run, and do not leave food or pet food outside.
alike: Red fox: Red coat, black legs, white tail tip

title: Red fox
def: The red fox is a small wild canine with a red coat, black legs, and a white tail tip.
look: red coat, black legs, white tail tip
bushy tail longer than half its body
use: Watch from a distance; foxes are usually shy.
not: A fox that is bold, stumbling, or aggressive may have rabies; leave it and report it.
alike: Coyote: Slim dog-like with a bushy low tail and pointed ears

title: Bobcat
def: The bobcat is a medium wild cat with a short bobbed tail, tufted ears, and a spotted coat.
look: short tail with a black tip, tufted ears, spotted coat
tail tip black on top, white below
use: Bobcats avoid people; enjoy the sighting from where you are.
not: Do not corner one, and treat a bold, unafraid bobcat as possibly rabid.

title: Porcupine
def: The porcupine is a slow, round rodent covered in barbed quills.
look: round quill-covered body, slow waddle
chewed bark high on trees
use: Leave it alone and keep dogs away. A pet with quills needs a vet.
not: It cannot throw quills, but it will swing its tail. Do not pull quills with bare fingers. Quills cannot be thrown. Keep dogs away.

title: Raccoon
def: The raccoon is a gray, masked, ring-tailed animal that raids camps and trash at night.
look: black mask and ringed tail
handprint-like tracks near water
use: Lock food away at night and keep a clean camp.
not: A raccoon active in daylight, stumbling or unafraid may have rabies; leave it and report it.

title: Striped skunk
def: The striped skunk is a black animal with white stripes down its back that sprays a strong musk when threatened.
look: black with white stripes down the back
stamps its feet and raises its tail before spraying
use: Back away slowly if it stamps or turns.
not: A skunk out in daylight acting oddly may have rabies.

title: Beaver
def: The beaver is a large water rodent with a flat paddle tail that builds dams and lodges.
look: flat paddle tail, dam and cut sapling stumps
tooth-chewed pointed stumps near water
use: Beaver ponds flood trails and make routes longer; plan around them.
not: Treat water near beaver ponds before drinking; it often carries Giardia ("beaver fever").

title: Snowshoe hare
def: The snowshoe hare is a northern hare with huge furry hind feet whose coat turns white in winter.
look: large back feet, coat white in winter and brown in summer
brown in summer, white in winter
use: Hares are legal small game in many states; check your state's rules.
not: Wear gloves when cleaning any rabbit or hare and cook it through, because of tularemia.

title: Wild turkey
def: The wild turkey is a large dark bird with a bare red-blue head and a fanned tail.
look: large dark bird with a bare head and fanned tail
toms gobble in spring
use: Turkey season has its own rules; identify the bird and what is beyond it before every shot.
not: Do not wear red, white, or blue in spring turkey woods; those are a gobbler's colors.

title: Ruffed grouse
def: The ruffed grouse is a brown or gray barred woodland bird with a fan tail and a dark neck ruff.
look: brown barred bird with a fan tail and dark neck ruff
drumming sound like a starting engine in spring
use: Grouse are upland game in New England; check season rules.
not: Cook game birds through.

title: Bald eagle
def: The bald eagle is a large raptor whose adults have a white head and tail and a yellow bill.
look: large dark bird with a white head and tail on adults
young birds are mottled brown for four years
use: Watch and photograph from a distance, especially near nests.
not: Bald eagles and their feathers are protected by federal law; do not disturb, collect, or harm them.

title: Great horned owl
def: The great horned owl is a large owl with ear tufts, yellow eyes, and a deep hooting call.
look: large owl with ear tufts and yellow eyes
white throat patch
use: Enjoy it from a distance, especially near nests in late winter.
not: Owls are federally protected; do not disturb, collect, or harm them.
ask: Tell me about great horned owl

title: Canada goose
def: The Canada goose is a large goose with a black neck and head and a white chin strap.
look: black neck and head with a white chin strap
V-shaped flocks with loud honking
use: Geese are migratory birds with federal and state season rules; check both.
not: Geese defend nests and goslings by charging; give them room.

title: Rattlesnake
def: The timber rattlesnake is a heavy-bodied venomous snake with a broad triangular head and a rattle on its tail.
look: thick body, triangular head, a rattle on the tail
dark crossbands on a yellow or dark body
use: Rattlesnakes are rare and protected in much of New England. Back away slowly and walk around.
not: Do not handle, kill, or pin it. After a bite, call 911, keep the person still and calm, and do not cut, suck, or tourniquet the bite. Venomous. Back away slowly. Call emergency services after a bite.
alike: Garter snake: Slim, three pale stripes along the body
Northern water snake: Banded brown snake near water. Not venomous but it bites hard. Often mistaken for a copperhead
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Copperhead
def: The copperhead is a venomous snake with a copper-colored head and tan hourglass bands.
look: copper head, tan body with hourglass bands
bands narrow on the back and wide on the sides
use: Copperheads live in southern New England's rocky woods. Back away slowly.
not: Do not handle it. After a bite, call 911, keep still, and do not cut, suck, or ice the bite. Venomous. Back away slowly. Call emergency services after a bite.
alike: Northern water snake: Banded brown snake near water. Not venomous but it bites hard. Often mistaken for a copperhead
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Cottonmouth
def: The cottonmouth is a heavy, dark venomous water snake that gapes to show a white mouth.
look: heavy dark water snake with a white mouth when it gapes
swims with its body high on the water
use: Cottonmouths do not live in New England; a dark snake in water there is almost always a northern water snake.
not: Do not handle any snake you cannot identify. After a bite, call 911 and keep still. Venomous. Back away slowly. Call emergency services after a bite.
alike: Northern water snake: Banded brown snake near water. Not venomous but it bites hard. Often mistaken for a copperhead
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Garter snake
def: The eastern garter snake is a slim, harmless snake with three pale stripes along its body.
look: slim, three pale stripes along the body
often basks on paths and rocks
use: It is harmless; let it go on its way.
not: Do not grab it; it may bite and release musk.
alike: Rattlesnake: Thick body, triangular head, a rattle on the tail. Venomous. Back away slowly. Call emergency services after a bite
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Northern water snake
def: The northern water snake is a common, non-venomous banded brown snake found in and near water.
look: banded brown snake near water
round pupils
use: It is not venomous; give it room.
not: It bites hard if handled, and it is often mistaken for a copperhead or cottonmouth. Not venomous but it bites hard. Often mistaken for a copperhead.
alike: Copperhead: Copper head, tan body with hourglass bands. Venomous. Back away slowly. Call emergency services after a bite
Cottonmouth: Heavy dark water snake with a white mouth when it gapes. Venomous. Back away slowly. Call emergency services after a bite
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Blacklegged (deer) tick
def: The blacklegged tick, or deer tick, is a tiny dark tick that spreads Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, and babesiosis.
look: tiny dark tick
adult females have an orange-red body and black plate
nymphs are the size of a poppy seed
use: Check your whole body after time outside, and remove ticks with fine tweezers pulled straight out.
not: Do not twist, burn, or smother a tick. See a clinician for a spreading rash or fever after a bite. Carries Lyme and other diseases. Remove with tweezers close to the skin and keep the date.
alike: American dog tick: Larger brown tick with white-cream markings on the back. Can carry spotted fever. Remove with tweezers close to the skin
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: American dog tick
def: The American dog tick is a larger brown tick with cream markings that can carry Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
look: larger brown tick with white-cream markings on the back
common in grassy fields and trail edges
use: Remove it with fine tweezers close to the skin and wash the bite.
not: See a clinician for fever, rash, or headache in the two weeks after a bite. Can carry spotted fever. Remove with tweezers close to the skin.
alike: Blacklegged (deer) tick: Tiny dark tick; adult females have an orange-red body and black plate. Carries Lyme and other diseases. Remove with tweezers close to the skin and keep the date
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.
ask: Tell me about american dog tick

title: Lone star tick
def: The lone star tick is a reddish-brown tick whose females have one white dot on the back; its bites are linked to a red-meat allergy.
look: reddish-brown tick with one white dot on the back of females
aggressive biter, spreading north
use: Remove it with fine tweezers close to the skin.
not: See a clinician for fever or rash after a bite, or hives hours after eating red meat. Bites can cause meat allergy. Remove with tweezers close to the skin.
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.
ask: Tell me about lone star tick

title: Black widow
def: The black widow is a shiny black spider with a red hourglass under its belly whose bite needs medical care.
look: shiny black spider with a red hourglass underneath
messy webs under rocks, logs, and outhouse seats
use: Shake out gloves, boots, and firewood before use.
not: After a bite, clean it, apply a cool pack, and get medical care, especially for cramps or trouble breathing. Venomous. Seek care after a bite.
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Bald-faced hornet
def: The bald-faced hornet is a black-and-white wasp that builds a gray paper nest in trees and defends it fiercely.
look: black and white wasp with a grey paper nest the size of a football
nests hang from branches or eaves
use: Walk wide around nests.
not: Call 911 for swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing after a sting. Stings hurt and are dangerous if allergic.
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Yellowjacket
def: The yellowjacket is a black-and-yellow wasp that nests in the ground and stings repeatedly.
look: black and yellow wasp that nests underground
busy hole in the ground
use: Watch for ground nests when clearing a camp or trail.
not: Call 911 for swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing after a sting. Stings hurt and are dangerous if allergic.
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a venomous bite; see a clinician for fever or rash after a tick bite.

title: Wild boar (feral hog)
def: The wild boar, or feral hog, is a dark bristly pig with a long snout that can be aggressive.
look: dark bristly pig with a long snout
rooted-up ground
use: Feral hogs are not established in New England; report one to your state wildlife agency.
not: Cook the meat fully, and wear gloves when cleaning; hogs can carry brucellosis. Can be aggressive. Cook the meat fully.
